summary.one_line: A four-year-old Surat maker of lab-grown-diamond (LGD) studded gold jewellery that mostly sells B2B. Revenue has grown fast (Rs.53.7 cr in FY24 to about Rs.203 cr in FY26), but operating cash flow has been negative for three straight years and customers and suppliers are highly concentrated. There is no clear moat in a crowded, deflating LGD market, and the Rs.108 cr fresh issue mainly pays for more working capital.
bull_points: Revenue from operations roughly doubled in each of the last two years: Rs.53.66 cr in FY24, Rs.96.85 cr in FY25 and Rs.202.89 cr in FY26. EBITDA margin rose from 10.21% to 15.27% and PAT reached Rs.22.32 cr (S5, S1, S4, S13).
The entire issue is fresh (no offer for sale), so all Rs.108 cr goes to the company rather than to exiting shareholders. Rs.70 cr is earmarked for working capital (S4, S16, S1).
Customer concentration is easing. The top-10 customers' share of revenue fell from 97.17% in FY23 to 84.24% in FY24, 76.68% in FY25 and 55.49% in FY26, across 323 B2B customers in FY26 (S1, S9).
Leverage is moderate: FY26 debt-to-equity of 0.29 and total borrowings of about Rs.23.4 cr against equity of Rs.79.4 cr (S7, S4).
bear_points: Operating cash flow was negative in every year even as profits grew: outflows of Rs.1.05 cr (FY24), Rs.10.05 cr (FY25) and Rs.14.73 cr (FY26), against cumulative FY24-26 PAT of about Rs.36 cr (S6, S4).
Purchases are highly concentrated: top-10 suppliers made up 86.16% of FY26 purchases and the single largest supplier 55.11% (S6).

The company only just qualified for the profitability-based listing route. It cleared the Rs.15 cr average operating-profit test by Rs.13.9 lakh (0.93%), and only after FY23 dropped out of the three-year window (S5).
LGD prices are deflating fast: from about $389/ct in 2022 to about $71/ct in 2026, with wholesale prices down 14% YoY in Q1 2026. That pressures ticket sizes and inventory values (S20, S19).

The SEBI-filed draft abridged prospectus contains apparent copy-paste errors. It describes two factories in Roorkee, Uttarakhand, offices in Delhi/Noida and a Nepal branch, while its own risk factor says the single plant is in Surat. That points to weak diligence on the offer document (S1).
watch_points: Whether the Rs.70 cr of working-capital money turns into positive operating cash flow, or simply funds a projected jump in working capital from Rs.44.95 cr (FY26) to Rs.110.31 cr (FY27) (S6, S15).
Whether the cash-credit line (96.59% drawn as of 31-Aug-2026, secured by promoter-owned property and personal guarantees) is paid down after the issue (S7).
Reported FY26 trade receivables differ between sources (Rs.16.06 cr vs Rs.21.46 cr). Check the RHP balance sheet (S6, S11).
Final subscription mix by category. Anchor allocation details were not found at the time of writing (S16, S17).

reasoning: The money raised funds a cash-hungry model rather than an asset that builds a moat. Rs.70 cr goes to working capital, and management itself projects the working-capital requirement rising from Rs.44.95 cr to Rs.110.31 cr in FY27 (S16, S6, S15). Three straight years of negative operating cash flow (Rs.14.73 cr outflow in FY26) while PAT more than doubled means the reported profit is not yet turning into cash (S6).

There is no demonstrable moat. Setting LGDs into 14k/18k gold is a low-barrier activity in a Surat cluster full of competitors. Well-funded brands such as GIVA and Limelight compete for the same consumer, and GIVA is also named as one of Nityas's key B2B customers (S9, S15, S22). The only 'barrier' claimed is a 32,000-design library and CAD/CAM capability, which rivals can replicate (S9).

The underlying commodity is deflating structurally. LGD prices fell roughly 82% between 2022 and 2026, and wholesale prices are still falling double digits with no floor, as Chinese supply rises (S20, S19). A B2B manufacturer holding Rs.41 cr of inventory is exposed to both LGD and gold price swings (S6).

Concentration is high on both sides. The top-10 suppliers provided 86.16% of purchases (one supplier 55.11%), the top-10 customers took 55.49% of revenue, and five states made up 85.03% of revenue in FY26 (S6, S9).

Governance and track record are thin. The company was incorporated in April 2022. Two of the three promoters have no formal education and 5 years of experience or less in the industry (Dhruv Savaliya about 4, Sonalben Chanchad about 5), though Rajnikant Chanchad has 20+ years (S18, S1). The listing test was cleared by Rs.13.9 lakh (S5). Pre-IPO investor special rights revive if the listing slips (S8). The abridged prospectus has factual errors about the company's own facilities (S1). Together these argue for waiting for several quarters of audited listed-company results before committing money.

subsections.title: What the company makes and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: Nityas designs, manufactures and sells gold jewellery (14k and 18k) studded with lab-grown diamonds. The range covers rings, earrings, pendants, bracelets, mangalsutras, nose pins, necklaces, cufflinks and bangles, and focuses on 'lightweight and affordable' daily-wear, occasion, men's and customised pieces (S1, S15). It was incorporated as a private company in Surat on 26 April 2022 and converted to a public company in July 2025 (S18).

Revenue comes from two segments. The first is B2B manufacturing and distribution to organised retailers and brands, standalone retailers and wholesalers. The second is D2C omnichannel retail through the subsidiary Ayaani Diamonds and Jewellery Pvt Ltd, which was acquired in July 2025 and consolidated only from then (S1). In FY26, B2B produced Rs.193.92 cr (95.58% of revenue) and D2C Rs.8.81 cr (4.34%) (S9). In practice this is a B2B contract/wholesale manufacturer with a small retail business attached.

blocks.caption: Segment revenue mix (Rs. million; restated consolidated)

blocks.text: Sources: FY23-H1 FY26 from the draft abridged prospectus (S1). The FY26 row comes from a secondary summary of the RHP (S9), because the full RHP (over 10 MB) could not be fetched.

Manufacturing is done at a single facility of about 7,000 sq ft in Surat, Gujarat. According to the company's IPO press release, its production capacity is about 360 kg a year (S13, S9). The work is done in-house by 122 karigars (artisans), supported by a 29-member design team working on CAD/CAM, and the company claims a library of 32,000+ designs (S9, S13). Total headcount was 192 as of 31 August 2026 (S4).

blocks.caption: Operating volumes (from DRHP KPIs)
rows: LGD-studded gold jewellery sold (kg, excl. diamond weight)

blocks.text: Against a stated capacity of about 360 kg a year (S13), FY25 sales of about 101 kg and H1 FY26 sales of about 84 kg (S1) suggest meaningful headroom. That fits with the IPO asking for no capex money. The capacity figure is a company claim, and a utilisation disclosure for FY26 could not be verified.

The D2C arm (Ayaani) runs an online store and 10 physical stores in 8 cities: Ahmedabad, Surat, Mathura, Delhi, Chandigarh, Jodhpur, Raipur and Udaipur. Seven are company-operated and three are franchises (S13, S11). Exports are small and order-driven, to the UAE, Australia, Canada, Taiwan and Kenya. Domestic markets were 96.87% of H1 FY26 revenue (S1).

In the SEBI-filed draft abridged prospectus, the 'Key manufacturing facilities' paragraph says the company runs two factories in Roorkee, Uttarakhand, with offices in Delhi and Noida and a branch in Nepal. The same document's risk factors, and every other source, say the only facility is in Surat (S1, S13). This looks like text carried over from another issuer's document. It is not evidence of wrongdoing, but it is a red flag about the care taken over the offer document.

subsections.title: Customers, suppliers and the supply chain

blocks.text: The supply chain is short. The company buys gold bullion and polished lab-grown diamonds, which together were 88.38%-99.26% of raw-material purchases across FY23 to H1 FY26 (S1). It designs and casts/sets the jewellery in Surat and sells on credit to retailers. The company says the B2B model needs upfront payment for bullion and diamonds before it collects from customers, and that is the root of its working-capital strain (S6).

Named key B2B customers include GIVA, Palmonas, ONYA and Ladia Diamonds (S15). The customer base has widened: 323 B2B customers in FY26 (S9), and the top-10 customer share fell from 97.17% (FY23) to 55.49% (FY26) (S1, S9). Revenue is still concentrated by region. Gujarat, Karnataka, Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra made up 82.27% of H1 FY26 revenue (S1), and five states made up 85.03% in FY26 (S9).

More than half of all purchases come from a single supplier (55.11% in FY26) (S6). The supplier is not named in the sources reviewed. Whether it is an unrelated bullion dealer or bank, or a related LGD grower, could not be confirmed. Investors should look this up in the RHP's 'Our Business' and RPT sections.

The CareEdge industry report commissioned for the offer puts the Indian gems and jewellery industry at about Rs.9,99,800 cr in CY25 and projects a 12.8% CAGR to CY30. It says the LGD jewellery segment grew at a 20.4% CAGR over CY20-25, with the global LGD jewellery market at $6,117 mn in CY25 (S9). The DRHP says the sector is about 7% of India's GDP and about 15% of merchandise exports (S1).

An independent estimate is much smaller for India specifically. Future Market Insights puts the Indian LGD jewellery market at about $453.7 mn in 2026, growing 14.8% a year to about $1,798.6 mn by 2036 (S21). Nityas's FY26 revenue of about Rs.203 cr (S5) would be a meaningful single-digit share of the India LGD jewellery market on that estimate. However, market definitions differ between reports, and no market-share claim by the company was found.

The drivers named in the DRHP are younger buyers wanting affordable, 'ethical' diamonds, rising incomes, growth in Tier-2/3 cities and more branded, omnichannel retail. It also names perception issues and price volatility as challenges (S1).

subsections.title: Price deflation: the key industry fact

blocks.text: The most important feature of this industry for an investor is that the product keeps getting cheaper. Business Standard reports LGD prices fell from about $388.77/ct in 2022 to about $71.13/ct in Jan-May 2026 (about 82%), and India's LGD export value fell even as volumes rose more than fourfold. Chinese producers supply more than 60% of global synthetic diamonds (S20). The Edahn Golan data reported by AIDI shows wholesale LGD prices down another 14% YoY in Q1 2026, rough CVD trading at $20-25/ct with reports of loss-making deals, and a market that 'remains oversupplied' with no clear price floor (S19).

items: Cheaper stones widen the addressable market (more buyers can afford diamond jewellery). This is the bull case behind Nityas's volume growth (S1, S19).
Falling stone prices also mean falling rupee value per piece and inventory write-down risk for anyone holding diamond stock. Nityas carried about Rs.41 cr of inventory at FY26 (S6).

Gold makes up much of the value of each piece. Rising gold prices inflate revenue without necessarily increasing volume, and gold volatility is a separate risk. The DRHP names availability and price of LGDs and gold bullion as a top-10 risk (S1).

blocks.text: Some of the revenue growth may reflect gold-price inflation rather than volume alone. In FY25, gold processed rose 48% (42.96 kg to 63.63 kg) while revenue rose 80% (S1). A volume-versus-price split for FY26 could not be verified.

subsections.title: Competitors and whether there is a moat

blocks.text: Competition comes from three directions: (1) hundreds of Surat/Mumbai LGD jewellery manufacturers doing similar B2B work; (2) funded consumer brands such as GIVA (over Rs.530 cr raised, 280+ stores, with an LGD line called 'Heer') and Limelight (about 40 outlets plus 40 shop-in-shops, $11 mn raised in 2025) (S22); and (3) listed diamond-jewellery exporters named by reviewers as peers, namely Goldiam International, Renaissance Global and Golkunda Diamonds & Jewellery, which one reviewer calls not truly comparable (S11, S12). The reviewer also describes the segment as 'over-crowded' (S11).

The company's claimed strengths are an integrated B2B plus D2C model, in-house manufacturing, design and CAD/CAM capability, and a diversified customer base (S1). None of these is a regulatory, technological or scale barrier. There is no import-substitution angle, no 'only Indian maker' claim, and no stated market-share leadership. The one reputational highlight, a lotus piece of lab-grown diamonds crafted by the promoter's team that flew on Skyroot's Vikram-1 rocket, is marketing rather than a moat (S23).

Verdict on moat: none demonstrated. Nityas is a fast-growing contract/wholesale manufacturer in a low-barrier, deflating category. Some of its largest-named customers (e.g. GIVA) are also brands that compete in the same end-consumer market as its own Ayaani D2C arm (S15, S22). Its bargaining power over both customers and a supplier base where one vendor provides 55% of purchases appears limited (S6).

FY23-H1 FY26 are from the DRHP abridged prospectus (S1). FY26 revenue/EBITDA/PAT are from secondary summaries of the RHP (S5, S13, S4). FY26 total income is Rs.203.33 cr (S4). One secondary source shows FY25 PAT as Rs.7.988 cr (S5), while the DRHP and other sources show Rs.9.79 cr (S1, S4). The DRHP figure is used here.

Growth has been steep: revenue rose about 17x in three years and PAT about 90x from a tiny FY23 base (S1, S5). Margins have risen steadily, which the company attributes to scaling. The FY26 EBITDA margin of 15.27% (S13) is high for a B2B jewellery manufacturer, whose margins are normally thin because gold is a pass-through. It deserves scrutiny: some of it may come from inventory gains on gold that rose in price, although that could not be confirmed. The company itself cautions in the RHP that 'historical revenue growth, margins and profitability may not be sustained' (S5).

Return ratios are falling as capital is added. ROCE declined from 88.44% (FY24) to 63.18% (FY25) and 42.93% (FY26) (S1, S11). Part of this is a denominator effect of equity raised in FY25-26, but it also shows the capital intensity of the model once working capital is funded.

subsections.title: Cash flow versus profit: the central red flag

blocks.caption: Cash flow and working capital (Rs. crore)

blocks.text: Sources: DRHP (S1) for FY23-H1 FY26 cash flows, H1 FY26 receivables and working capital; RHP-based summaries (S6, S15) for FY24-FY26 inventory, receivables and working capital. *FY26 trade receivables are reported as Rs.16.06 cr by one source (S6) and Rs.21.46 cr by another (S11). This could not be resolved without the RHP.

Operating cash flow was negative in every year reported, even though the company earned about Rs.36 cr of cumulative PAT over FY24-FY26 (S4, S6). In FY26, inventory absorbed Rs.21.48 cr and receivables Rs.11.87 cr, and the Rs.14.73 cr operating outflow was covered by Rs.16.86 cr of financing inflows (S6). Net working-capital days rose from 39 (FY23) to 47 (FY24), 105 (FY25) and 124 (H1 FY26). Debtor days rose from 16 to 35 over FY24-H1 FY26 (S1).

The company's explanation is that a scaling B2B jewellery business pays upfront for bullion and stones and extends credit to retailers (S6). That is plausible, and it is common for young jewellery manufacturers. But it means reported profits are, so far, entirely reinvested in stock and receivables. Shareholders have not yet seen a rupee of free cash flow.

Leverage is moderate on paper: FY26 debt/equity is 0.29 (S7, S4). Net worth rose mainly through fresh equity. The DRHP's weighted-average acquisition cost table shows shares issued in the last three years at prices up to Rs.40.91 (split/bonus adjusted) (S1), and the net worth jump to Rs.79.43 cr in FY26 (S4) was helped by that capital plus retained profit. Net worth figures differ slightly across secondary summaries (e.g. Rs.61.75 cr in one) (S5), probably because of definitions such as non-controlling interest.

Liquidity is tight. As of 31 August 2026, the YES Bank cash-credit line of Rs.13.58 cr was 96.59% drawn (Rs.13.12 cr outstanding). It is secured on stock, receivables and floors of Rathi House in Surat owned by promoter Rajnikant Chanchad, and is personally guaranteed by Rajnikant and Sonalben Chanchad and by Raj Dineshbhai Monpara (S7). Monpara is also a 4.08% pre-issue shareholder (S1). Contingent liabilities were Rs.2.88 cr at March 2026 (S11).
The statutory auditors expressed no qualification, reservation or emphasis of matter on the restated financials for the DRHP periods (S1).

blocks.text: The eligibility route changed between the DRHP and the RHP. The DRHP (dated 30 March 2026, cleared by SEBI in July 2026) filed under Regulation 6(2) because the company failed the profitability and net-tangible-asset tests. That route requires at least 75% QIB allocation and allows only 10% retail (S1, S3, S16). With FY26 added and FY23 removed from the look-back window, the RHP switched to Regulation 6(1): average operating profit was Rs.15.139 cr against the Rs.15 cr threshold, a margin of Rs.13.9 lakh. That allowed the retail quota to rise to 35% (S5).

Some platforms still show the old DRHP split of 75% QIB / 15% NII / 10% retail (S10). The RHP-based sources consistently show 50/15/35 (S4, S5, S14). Retail investors should check the split in the bidding app. The larger retail quota means retail investors will make up a larger part of the book, rather than there being a larger institutional check on price.

blocks.caption: Use of net proceeds
rows: Main object; about 65% of gross proceeds (S1, S16)
Balance, capped at 25% of gross proceeds (about Rs.27 cr maximum)
Exact figure not confirmed from RHP (S1)
The rest of the about Rs.108 cr gross

blocks.text: No OFS means no existing shareholder is cashing out through the issue, which is a positive: all the money goes to the company (S4). But the money is going to fund inventory and receivables. Secondary summaries of the RHP's working-capital estimate say the requirement rises from Rs.44.95 cr in FY26 to about Rs.110.31 cr in FY27 (S15, S6). In other words, the IPO is mainly a substitute for bank borrowing to pay for another year of rapid, cash-absorbing growth.

That is a legitimate use, but a weak one for a minority investor. Working-capital money does not create a durable asset or barrier. It only pays off if the business later converts those receivables and inventory into cash, which it has not yet done in any reported year (S6).

Promoters and the promoter group hold 58.1% before the issue and about 43.51% after it (S4, S14). The DRHP shows Rajnikant Chanchad at 52.06%, Sonalben Chanchad at 3.98%, promoter-group member Janakbhai N Savaliya at 2.10%, and the third promoter Dhruv Savaliya holding nothing (S1). Pre-IPO investors include Wealthwave Capital Trust (5.10%), Raj Dineshbhai Monpara (4.08%), SK Family Trust (3.83%) and Astha Aditya Kanodia (3.83%) (S1).

The weighted-average cost of shares acquired in the 18 months and 3 years before the DRHP was Rs.14.30, and in the last year Rs.18.42, with a range of nil to Rs.40.91 (adjusted for the 2:1 split and 10:1 bonus of March 2026) (S1). A reviewer puts the promoters' average acquisition cost at Rs.3.43-11.82 per share (S11). Against a Rs.75 issue price, IPO investors are paying far more than insiders did.

A 2025 share-purchase-cum-shareholders' agreement with Wealthwave Capital Fund and MG 369 Finventure gives those investors special rights: ROFR, tag-along, exit rights, events of default, and a director-nomination right if the IPO is not completed. These rights are held in abeyance and end on listing, but revive in full if the IPO misses its long-stop date (S8).

blocks.text: The board has six members. Besides the three promoters there are three independent directors: Dineshbhai Manjibhai Bhimani, Anu Ashish Amodia and Nair Ajit Velayudhan. The key managers are Company Secretary Manvi Meet Shah and CFO Denish Bharatbhai Kalyanpremchandwala (S1). The board is dominated by the Chanchad family and has the minimum 50% independent directors that a promoter-executive chair requires.

Rajnikant Chanchad has been publicly described as a Surat LGD dealer who takes premium export orders (for example watches and phone covers priced at Rs.2.5-14 lakh). He led the team that made the 'Cosmic Bloom' LGD lotus flown on Skyroot's Vikram-1 (S23). He clearly has deep trade experience. But the listed company is only about four years old (incorporated April 2022) (S18), so there is no multi-cycle track record for the company itself. No earlier listed venture by the promoters was found.

The full RPT schedule in the DRHP/RHP could not be read (the documents timed out or were too large to fetch), so a line-by-line RPT review is not possible here. The promoter linkages confirmed from secondary sources are these.

items: The company's bank borrowings are secured partly on floors of Rathi House, Surat, owned by promoter Rajnikant Chanchad. The registered office is on the 6th and 7th floors of the same building, so it appears the company operates from promoter-owned premises. Lease or rent terms were not verified (S1, S7).
Promoters Rajnikant and Sonalben Chanchad, plus pre-IPO shareholder Raj Dineshbhai Monpara, have given personal guarantees on the YES Bank facilities (S7, S1).

The subsidiaries are Ayaani Diamonds and Jewellery Pvt Ltd (the D2C arm, acquired July 2025) and Ratna LGD Pvt Ltd (S18, S1). The seller of Ayaani and the acquisition price could not be verified. Investors should check whether Ayaani was bought from a promoter-linked party.
Special rights of pre-IPO investors (Wealthwave, MG 369 Finventure) lapse on listing but can revive (S8).

blocks.text: No specific abusive RPT was found. But the RPT section, the identity of the 55% supplier and the Ayaani acquisition terms remain unverified. Given the thin secondary coverage, those are the three things a cautious applicant should read in the RHP before bidding.

blocks.caption: Outstanding litigation (as of DRHP)
rows: Nil criminal, tax, regulatory or civil; nil SEBI/exchange action in 5 years

blocks.text: The litigation profile is light. The tax claim is about 12% of FY26 PAT (S1, S4). The nature of the criminal case against the subsidiary is not described in the summary and should be checked. Contingent liabilities were Rs.2.88 cr at March 2026 (S11).

The offer document itself is a concern. The SEBI-filed draft abridged prospectus contains unresolved 'Error! Bookmark not defined.' cross-references and a customer-concentration table labelled '% of total purchases' that actually shows supplier data. It also includes a facilities paragraph (Roorkee plants, Delhi/Noida offices, Nepal branch) that contradicts the Surat single-plant disclosure (S1). The sole BRLM, Choice Capital, has a mixed record: one reviewer notes that 4 of its 12 IPOs in three years closed below the issue price on listing day (S11).

subsections.title: The risks that should drive the decision

items: Cash conversion: operating cash flow was negative for three years (Rs.14.73 cr outflow in FY26), and the working-capital need is projected to more than double to about Rs.110 cr in FY27. Growth may keep consuming cash and force more borrowing or equity (S6, S15).
Supplier dependence: one supplier provides 55.11% of purchases and the top-10 provide 86.16%. Any disruption or repricing hits the entire production chain (S6).

LGD price deflation and oversupply: prices are down about 82% since 2022 and wholesale prices are still falling double digits, driven by Chinese supply. That risks inventory losses, shrinking ticket sizes and margin pressure on B2B orders (S20, S19, S6).

Customer and regional concentration: the top-10 customers take 55.49% of revenue and five states 85.03%. Several key customers are consumer brands that could build or switch manufacturing easily (S9, S15).
Single-site operations: all manufacturing is in one Surat facility, so any fire, flood, labour or regulatory disruption stops output (S1, S9).

Sustainability of margins and growth: the company itself warns historical growth and margins may not be sustained. Listing eligibility was met by only Rs.13.9 lakh of average operating profit, which shows how new the profit scale is (S5).

Governance and diligence: the offer document has errors, some RPT and supplier details are unverified, promoter property is used as bank collateral, and pre-IPO investor rights revive if listing fails (S1, S7, S8).

blocks.text: Among the DRHP's own top-10 risks, the ones that are really specific to Nityas are customer, state and supplier concentration, reliance on LGD and gold prices, the single facility, working-capital intensity and rising receivables (Rs.4.06 cr in FY24 to Rs.26.37 cr at Sep-2025). Discretionary demand, seasonality and design risk are generic to all jewellery issuers (S1).
Taken together: the business is growing fast, but it is a price-taker on its main input, sells to a handful of regions and customers, and has not yet shown it can turn accounting profit into cash.

items: Customer concentration has fallen sharply over four years (top-10 from 97% to 55%) as the base grew to 323 B2B customers (S1, S9).
Stated capacity (about 360 kg a year) is well above recent sales volumes, so near-term growth does not depend on new capex (S13, S1).
Leverage is modest (debt/equity 0.29) and the fresh equity will reduce reliance on the nearly maxed-out cash-credit line (S7).
The auditors raised no qualifications, and there is no litigation against promoters or directors (S1).

blocks.text: These mitigants reduce the risk of outright distress but do not address the core issues of commodity deflation, no moat and weak cash conversion.

The offer document's stated strategies are to widen the B2B customer base, build the 'Ayaani' D2C omnichannel brand, focus on design-led product innovation and a broader portfolio, fund working capital to support growth, and pursue selective exports while keeping a domestic focus (S1).

The only quantified forward-looking figure found is the working-capital projection that underpins the objects of the issue: from Rs.44.95 cr (FY26) to about Rs.110.31 cr (FY27) (S15, S6). This implies management plans a further large step-up in business volume in FY27. No explicit revenue or margin guidance was found.

Public comments are generic. The IPO press release quotes the CMD calling the IPO 'an important milestone in our journey' to expand the customer base and manufacturing capabilities (S13). The RHP explicitly warns that historical growth, margins and profitability 'may not be sustained' (S5). No analyst call, interview with concrete targets, or store-rollout number for Ayaani was found.

Beyond the working-capital projection and the qualitative strategy list, management has given no concrete outlook. Anything more specific would be inference from past growth, which this report avoids.

items: Half-yearly operating cash flow: does it turn positive once the issue proceeds are deployed (S6)?
Gross and EBITDA margins as LGD prices keep falling (S19, S20).
Growth of D2C (Ayaani) revenue share from 4.34%, and store count beyond 10 (S9, S13).
Top supplier share (55% in FY26) and any disclosure of who that supplier is (S6).
Receivable days (35 in H1 FY26) and any write-offs (S1).

blocks.text: If two to four quarters of listed results show positive operating cash flow and stable margins despite LGD deflation, the case would improve materially. Until then, the growth story rests on management's unproven ability to fund working capital.

subsections.title: Day-1 status, anchors and grey market

blocks.text: This report was written on 30 September 2026, the day the issue opened. The subscription tracker checked shows 0x overall, with QIB/NII/retail data still awaiting the first exchange update. No meaningful subscription figures were available at the time of writing, and none should be inferred (S17). Institutional bids typically arrive on the final day.

The anchor book was scheduled for 29 September 2026 (S16). Anchor investor names, amounts allocated and lock-in details were not found in any source reviewed. The anchor allocation and its lock-in schedule for this issue are unconfirmed, and applicants should check the exchange's anchor-allocation notice.
GMP is an unofficial, unregulated indicator and has already fallen from Rs.9 to Rs.5 before bidding opened (S14). It is not an investment signal and played no part in the verdict.

method: Primary source: the SEBI-hosted draft abridged prospectus (a 9-page summary of the DRHP dated 30 March 2026), read page by page. It supplied FY23-FY25 and H1 FY26 restated financials, KPIs, segment mix, concentration, promoter profiles, shareholding, objects and litigation. The full DRHP on NSE archives timed out twice on fetch, and the RHP (company site and chittorgarh.net copies) was either unreachable or over the 10 MB fetch limit. So the full RPT schedule, the 'Our Business' chapter, the identity of the top supplier, the Ayaani acquisition terms and the exact general-corporate-purposes and issue-expense split could NOT be read directly. These gaps are flagged in the text. FY26 (year to March 2026) figures, the Regulation 6(1) eligibility switch, cash-flow detail, borrowings and security, and the working-capital projection come from secondary summaries of the RHP (Multibagg, Chittorgarh, Kotak Neo, IPO Watch, Univest, InvestorGain, the company press release on NewsX). They were cross-checked where possible: FY26 revenue, EBITDA and PAT agree across at least three sources. Discrepancies are disclosed rather than resolved: FY25 PAT in one source, FY26 net worth, FY26 trade receivables (Rs.16.06 cr vs Rs.21.46 cr), FY26 borrowings (Rs.23.42 cr used, since it reconciles with the 0.29 debt/equity; Chittorgarh shows Rs.9.08 cr), and the QIB/retail split (one platform still shows DRHP-era 75/10). Industry context uses the CareEdge figures cited in the offer summaries plus independent LGD pricing data (AIDI/Edahn Golan, Business Standard) and market-size data (Future Market Insights). Some sources (S3, S20-S23) were seen in search results rather than opened in full. Valuation figures reported by sources (P/E, P/B, market cap) were deliberately excluded. Subscription data is day-1 and effectively empty. Anchor allocation was not found.
